title: Guild trends did not hide warming in North American bird communities (BBS 1966-2025); with unshrunk trends, populations shifted to cool range parts at 20-40% of spatial expectation, mainly after 1995
abstract: Question: bird community temperature indices (CTI) from the North American Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) follow less than 10% of the change that their spatial gradients predict. Data: USGS hierarchical BBS trends 1966-2025 for 309 land-bird species in 30 Bird Conservation Regions (BCRs), BBS 2026 route counts, GHCN_CAMS and Berkeley Earth temperature, AVONET guild classes and song frequency. Method: (1) pre-registered: a weighted regression split the BCR CTI change from species trends into a guild part (habitat, migration, diet, aerial insectivore, introduced) and a within-guild part; species bootstrap and a trait-shuffle null. (2) Secondary and exploratory: our own unshrunk BCR trends (Poisson, route x observer groups); slopes of species x BCR trends on the trend that each species' own BCR abundance-temperature profile predicts, within and between species; tests of scaling with BCR warming and with time (1966-1995 against 1996-2025). Results: guild trends did not hide thermophilisation: masking share 0.11 (95% CI -0.24 to 0.30; shuffle null p = 0.38), near 0 with log weights or raw trends. Abundance-weighted CTI ratios were dominated by a few colonial species (species-bootstrap interval about -0.7 to 0.8). The USGS model kept only about one third of within-species regional trend contrasts (slope 0.34 against raw trends). With raw trends, species followed 0.39 (0.26-0.53) of their profile expectation pooled, 0.20 (0.02-0.40) within species and 0.48 (0.28-0.68) between species (0.45 with guild and song-frequency controls); USGS trends gave 0.23, 0.03 and 0.33. The shift did not scale with BCR warming differences, but these differences were poorly measured (GHCN_CAMS against Berkeley Earth r = 0.67). In time, the shift was near 0 in 1966-1995 (lambda 0.12 pooled, -0.03 within) and 0.42 (0.31-0.54) pooled and 0.24 (0.05-0.42) within species in 1996-2025, while warming increased only 1.5 times; profiles from 1966-1985 counts gave the same result. Conclusion: guild trends are not the missing process; much of the apparent gap comes from CTI weighting and model shrinkage, and the remaining response builds up with a lag that the data do not determine (lag-model tau 5 to more than 300 years). Limitations: correlational; two periods only; changes in survey coverage between periods; raw trends have no detection model; hearing drift remains in pooled and between-species values; the scaling tests and period split were added after the first results.

Left: route-mean May-July temperature. Middle: cool-ward shift rate k per period (pooled and within species, raw-count trends) against the warming rate. Right: ratio of late to early shift in a first-order lag model as a function of tau, with the observed pooled ratio.
